values.label: Blood pH (arterial)
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3: “Reference values (arterial): pH: 7.35–7.45” and Metabolic Acidosis: “At the normal pH of 7.40, the ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid buffer is 20:1.”
values.note: The section's opening also says: “Normal arterial blood pH is restricted to a very narrow range of 7.35 to 7.45.”

values.label: Carbon dioxide partial pressure (PCO2), arterial, male
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3: “pCO 2 : male: 35–48 mm Hg, female: 32–45 mm Hg”
values.note: The model has one carbon dioxide level; it is compared with both the male and the female range.

values.label: Carbon dioxide partial pressure (PCO2), arterial, female
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3: “pCO 2 : male: 35–48 mm Hg, female: 32–45 mm Hg”
values.note: Same model marker as the male row.

values.label: Total bicarbonate (HCO3–), venous
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3: “total venous bicarbonate: 22–29 mM.”
values.note: The source gives this range for venous blood, while its pH and carbon dioxide ranges are arterial. The model has a single blood bicarbonate level.

values.label: Bicarbonate to carbonic acid ratio
values.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.4 Acid-Base Balance, Bicarbonate-Carbonic Acid Buffer: “Bicarbonate ions and carbonic acid are present in the blood in a 20:1 ratio if the blood pH is within the normal range.”
values.note: A single value, not a range. The model stands in for carbonic acid with dissolved carbon dioxide (0.03 × PCO2, a constant of the model's equation, not of the cited excerpts).

states.label: Metabolic acidosis (primary bicarbonate deficiency)
states.summary: Too little bicarbonate makes the blood too acidic; breathing can then speed up to drive off carbon dioxide and bring the ratio back toward normal.

shiftNotes.pco2m: normal at first, then lower if the lungs compensate
shiftNotes.pco2f: normal at first, then lower if the lungs compensate

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3 (columns pH, PCO2, total HCO3–): “pH PCO 2 Total HCO 3 – Metabolic acidosis ↓ N, then ↓ ↓” and “Metabolic acidosis occurs when the blood is too acidic (pH below 7.35) due to too little bicarbonate, a condition called primary bicarbonate deficiency.”
states.modelNote: The model lowers bicarbonate and lets the lungs partly compensate.

states.label: Respiratory acidosis (primary carbon dioxide excess)
states.summary: Breathing that cannot clear enough carbon dioxide leaves too much carbonic acid in the blood; the kidneys can then conserve more bicarbonate.

shiftNotes.hco3: normal at first, then higher if the kidneys compensate

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3 (columns pH, PCO2, total HCO3–): “Respiratory acidosis ↓ ↑ N, then ↑” and “Respiratory acidosis occurs when the blood is overly acidic due to an excess of carbonic acid, resulting from too much CO 2 in the blood.”
states.modelNote: The model raises carbon dioxide and lets the kidneys partly compensate.

states.label: Metabolic alkalosis (primary bicarbonate excess)
states.summary: Too much bicarbonate makes the blood too alkaline; breathing can slow to keep more carbon dioxide, though the lungs compensate less well for alkalosis.

shiftNotes.pco2m: normal at first, then higher if the lungs compensate
shiftNotes.pco2f: normal at first, then higher if the lungs compensate

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3 (columns pH, PCO2, total HCO3–): “Metabolic alkalosis ↑ N, then↑ ↑” and “It occurs when the blood is too alkaline (pH above 7.45) due to too much bicarbonate (called primary bicarbonate excess).” Compensation: “Hence, the respiratory route is less efficient at compensating for metabolic alkalosis than for acidosis.”
states.modelNote: The model raises bicarbonate and lets the lungs partly compensate, less strongly than for acidosis.

states.label: Respiratory alkalosis (primary carbon dioxide deficiency)
states.summary: Breathing deeper or faster than needed blows off carbon dioxide, so the blood becomes too alkaline; the kidneys can then eliminate more bicarbonate.

shiftNotes.hco3: normal at first, then lower if the kidneys compensate

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.3 (columns pH, PCO2, total HCO3–): “Respiratory alkalosis ↑ ↓ N, then ↓” and “Respiratory alkalosis occurs when the blood is overly alkaline due to a deficiency in carbonic acid and CO 2 levels in the blood.”
states.modelNote: The model lowers carbon dioxide and lets the kidneys partly compensate.

states.label: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor diuretics
states.summary: Blocking carbonic anhydrase in the kidney means less bicarbonate is returned to the blood, so blood bicarbonate falls.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.4 Acid-Base Balance, Renal Regulation of Acid-Base Balance: “A decrease of blood bicarbonate can result from the inhibition of carbonic anhydrase by certain diuretics or from excessive bicarbonate loss due to diarrhea.” pH direction from section 26.5, Metabolic Acidosis: “Metabolic acidosis occurs when the blood is too acidic (pH below 7.35) due to too little bicarbonate, a condition called primary bicarbonate deficiency.”
states.modelNote: The model lowers bicarbonate as for metabolic acidosis; the cited passages give no direction for carbon dioxide.

states.label: Diuretics for hypertension (potassium depletion)
states.summary: Diuretics used for high blood pressure can deplete potassium; with less potassium, more hydrogen ions are exchanged in the kidney and more bicarbonate is conserved.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Metabolic Alkalosis: “Other causes of metabolic alkalosis include the loss of hydrochloric acid from the stomach through vomiting, potassium depletion due to the use of diuretics for hypertension, and the excessive use of laxatives.” and “It occurs when the blood is too alkaline (pH above 7.45) due to too much bicarbonate (called primary bicarbonate excess).” Kidney mechanism from section 26.4: “If there is less potassium, more hydrogen ions enter the filtrate to be exchanged with sodium and more bicarbonate is conserved.” and “Thus, lost chloride results in an increased reabsorption of bicarbonate by the renal system.”
states.modelNote: The model raises bicarbonate as for metabolic alkalosis. The cited excerpts do not name loop or thiazide diuretics or describe volume contraction; they name diuretics for hypertension and potassium depletion.

states.label: Ingested bicarbonate or antacids (for example sodium bicarbonate)
states.summary: Taking in bicarbonate adds base directly, giving a transient excess of bicarbonate in the blood.
states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Metabolic Alkalosis: “A transient excess of bicarbonate in the blood can follow ingestion of excessive amounts of bicarbonate, citrate, or antacids for conditions such as stomach acid reflux—known as heartburn.” and “It occurs when the blood is too alkaline (pH above 7.45) due to too much bicarbonate (called primary bicarbonate excess).”
states.modelNote: The model raises bicarbonate as for metabolic alkalosis.

states.label: Salicylate (aspirin) toxicity
states.summary: Salicylic acid adds acid to the blood, and the hyperventilation that follows drives off carbon dioxide, so pH can move either way.

shiftNotes.ph: acidosis from the acid itself, then respiratory alkalosis can follow

states.where: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 26.5 Disorders of Acid-Base Balance, Table 26.2 Common Causes of Metabolic Acidosis: “Salicylate/aspirin Salicylic acid (SA)*” and “An overdose of aspirin causes acidosis due to the acidity of this metabolite.” and “Metabolic acidosis occurs when the blood is too acidic (pH below 7.35) due to too little bicarbonate, a condition called primary bicarbonate deficiency.” Respiratory Alkalosis: “Surprisingly, aspirin overdose—salicylate toxicity—can result in respiratory alkalosis as the body tries to compensate for initial acidosis.” Section 26.4: “Hypocapnia , or abnormally low blood levels of CO 2 , occurs with any cause of hyperventilation that drives off the CO 2 , such as salicylate toxicity, elevated room temperatures, fever, or hysteria.”
states.modelNote: The model lowers both bicarbonate and carbon dioxide, a mixed picture; it adds no further compensation.
